tools.name: plan_marketing_copy
tools.description: Plan any piece of marketing copy before you write it, whether it's an ad, a landing page, a sales page or sales letter, an email, a subject line, a social post, a headline or a video script. It takes the goal, the reader and the offer, and returns which of the nine questions every reader silently asks this piece has to answer, which ones deserve the most words for this reader, and a few ways to answer each one, drawn from real advertising and linked to the Persuasion Taxonomy. One option is always the established move and the rest are less expected.

goal.description: What the copy has to get the reader to do: purchase means buy now, signup means an opt-in, a trial, a demo or a lead form, click means the whole job is the click (most ads and links), and engagement covers nurture emails, newsletters and social posts that should be read, answered or followed.

format.description: The kind of copy it is: ad, landing_page, sales_letter for long-form sales copy, email, email_subject, social_post, video_script or headline.

audience.description: Who will read it, as specifically as you can put it: their role, their situation and what they already believe.

offer.description: What you're selling or asking for, and the main promise.

awareness_level.description: How much the reader already knows, on Eugene Schwartz's scale: unaware means they don't know they have the problem, problem_aware that they feel it, solution_aware that they know solutions exist, product_aware that they know you, and most_aware that they're ready and only need the offer.

category.description: The industry, for a comparison with what brands in that category usually do. There is enough data for apparel, automotive, b2b_saas, beauty_skincare, business_coaching, consumer_tech, dtc_food_bev, dtc_health, fitness_health, home_goods, info_product, investing, marketing_education, otc_pharma, personal_care, personal_development, supplements, weight_loss. Any other category still works, just without the comparison.

persuasion_mode.description: How hard the copy is allowed to push. Balanced is the default, persuasive and sustainable over time. Equity protects long-term trust, so it rules out fear, hype and hard-sell moves. Aggressive is for short-term direct response and allows fear, threat and hard scarcity. In every mode, the claims stay true.

options_per_question.description: How many ways to answer each question you want to see. The default is 4.

annotations.title: Plan marketing copy (the nine reader questions)

tools.name: diagnose_marketing_copy
tools.description: Review, critique or roast any piece of marketing copy, whether it's an ad, a landing page, an email, a sales page, a social post or a script, and find out why it might not persuade. It takes the copy and line-by-line labels naming the reader question each persuasive line answers. It returns which of the nine questions the copy answers for its goal, which it answers weakly and which it skips, along with the biggest gap and what readers do when it is missing. It also checks the order, whether the answers agree with each other, and the craft, pointing to the exact words that read as machine-written, like em dashes, "it's not X, it's Y" lines and sentences that all run the same length. Then it checks the opening line and suggests techniques from the catalog to fill the gap. It answers requests like "is this good?", "roast this", "what's wrong with this copy?" and "how do I make it better?"

tools.name: explain_why_not_converting
tools.description: Work out why an ad, a landing page, an email or a whole funnel isn't converting, starting from what you can see. Maybe people don't click (a low CTR), or they click and bounce, or they read and don't buy. Maybe they abandon the checkout or the form, the leads never buy, customers buy once and leave, or emails don't get opened or get opened and nobody clicks. Whatever the symptom, you get back the reader questions most likely going unanswered, what to check in the copy first, and the problems copy can't fix that you should rule out, along with techniques to try and the test that would confirm the diagnosis. It answers questions like why marketing "isn't working", "isn't converting" or "isn't selling", or why results dropped.

symptom.description: What you can see happening. Use low_click_through when people see it and don't click, high_bounce when they click and leave fast, reads_but_no_action when they read and don't convert, starts_but_abandons when they abandon the checkout or form, leads_dont_buy when signups never buy, buys_once_no_return for refunds, churn and no repeat orders, low_open_rate when emails don't get opened, and opens_no_clicks when they get opened but not clicked.

tools.name: find_persuasion_techniques
tools.description: Search the Persuasion Taxonomy, 767 named persuasion techniques documented from real advertising and organized by the nine reader questions they answer. It takes a plain description of what the copy should do, like handle a price objection, make an opening less generic, prove a claim or reframe a problem, and finds the techniques that do it. Each one comes with its name and ID, a one-line definition, a real example, how common it is in a category if you name one, and a link. It answers requests for tactics, angles or a less expected way to make a point.

query.description: What the copy should do, in plain words, like "handle a price objection".

question.description: Limits the results to techniques that answer one reader question.

format.description: The kind of copy it is: ad, landing_page, sales_letter for long-form sales copy, email, email_subject, social_post, video_script or headline.

Any other category still works, just without the comparison.

tools.name: get_persuasion_technique
tools.description: Look up one persuasion technique by its ID (like PT-PRV-10000), its slug or its name. You get the full definition, why it works, when it lands and when it backfires, real examples from advertising, related and opposite techniques, and a link you can cite. It answers questions like what a tactic is called or how it works.

tools.name: check_headlines
tools.description: Check headlines, email subject lines, ad openings, video hooks, social post openings and first lines, and compare options against each other. For each line it tells you whether the line does its job in that spot, meaning which of the nine reader questions it answers, and whether a competitor could send it unchanged. It also shows exactly what a reader sees before the cutoff, flags anything that fails outright, and brings in evidence from thousands of real headline tests. Then it says what each option is betting on and which two to test. It answers requests to check or choose between headlines, hooks or subject lines, including "which one is best?" You won't get a score out of ten. Nobody can predict a winner from the words alone, and that includes this tool.

slot.description: Where the lines will appear: email_subject, ad_opening, landing_page_headline, first_line, video_hook, social_post_open, sales_letter_headline. Each spot has its own job, and the check tells you what it is.

question.description: The reader question the text answers, by its role name: DISRUPT for "Why am I even reading this?", IDENTIFY for "Is this written for me?", AGITATE for "How bad is my problem, really?", REFRAME for "Am I thinking about this correctly?", PROVE for "Can I trust the claim?", ELEVATE for "What does my life look like after?", RESOLVE for "What's stopping me from saying yes?", COMPEL for "Why should I act right now?", BOND for "Do I like and trust who's speaking?".

words.description: The exact words in the line that answer it.

answers.description: The reader questions this line answers, each with the exact words that do it. Leave it empty if the line answers none.

offer.description: The deal or the ask, like the price, a discount, a trial or a deadline.

audience.description: Who reads it: their role, their situation and what is theirs.

proof.description: Real proof you can point to, like customer counts, results or names.

brief.description: The brief. The swap test needs it to tell whether a competitor could send the line unchanged, and without it no line can pass.

follows.description: What the reader saw just before this line, like the ad before a landing page headline, or the headline or subject before a first line.

awareness_level.description: How much the reader already knows, on Eugene Schwartz's scale: unaware means they don't know they have the problem, problem_aware that they feel it, solution_aware that they know solutions exist, product_aware that they know you, and most_aware that they're ready and only need the offer.

annotations.title: Check and compare headlines, hooks, and subject lines

tools.name: check_marketing_claims
tools.description: Check whether marketing claims and calls to action are specific enough to believe. It catches the vague superlative, like "the best" or "#1", that readers discount on sight. It catches promises with no proof behind them and results with no mechanism, and it flags the generic buttons everyone uses, like "Learn more" and "Get started". Then it says how to fix each one. It covers claims like "results in days", "trusted by thousands" or "the #1 tool", and any button text. For a headline, it checks the claim only, not whether the headline does its job in its spot.

text.description: The claim or the button text, exactly as written.

type.description: headline, cta (a button or call to action) or body_claim (a claim inside the copy).

context.description: For a claim in the body, the paragraph around it, so a mechanism named nearby still counts.

tools.name: plan_ab_test
tools.description: Plan an A/B test for marketing copy. It takes the current conversion rate, the smallest lift worth detecting and the daily traffic, and returns how many visitors each version needs and how many days to run. It also frames the test as two different answers to the same reader question, so the result teaches you something you can reuse, and not just that "B won". It answers questions like how long to run a test, how much traffic it needs, whether a test is worth running, or what to test next.

baseline_conversion_rate_percent.description: The current conversion rate, in percent, so 3 means 3% and 0.8 means 0.8%.

minimum_detectable_lift_percent.description: The smallest relative lift worth detecting, in percent. 20 means a 20% lift, like going from 3% to 3.6%.

daily_visitors.description: How many visitors a day enter the test, across all versions.

versions.description: How many versions, counting the original.

question.description: The reader question both versions answer, each in its own way.

tools.name: read_ab_test_result
tools.description: Read the result of an A/B test. You get each version's conversion rate and lift, whether the difference is statistically significant, the confidence interval, and the chance each version really beats the original. It also warns you about the things that make a test result lie. Those include too few conversions, traffic that didn't split the way it should (a sample ratio mismatch), stopping the moment it looked good, and testing too many versions at once. It answers questions like "did my test win?", "is this significant?", "which version won?" or "should I keep it running?"

versions.description: Each version with its visitors and conversions. Put the original, the control, first.

intended_split.description: How you meant to split the traffic, like [50, 50]. The default is an even split.

question.description: The reader question the versions answered in different ways.

instructions:
This is the Persuasion Taxonomy, from Coppica. It gives you a working model of the reader, a catalog of 767 persuasion techniques documented from real advertising, a way to check copy before anyone sees it, and the math behind A/B tests.

The model of the reader is simple. Everyone who reads an ad, a page or an email is silently asking nine questions: Why am I even reading this? Is this written for me? How bad is my problem, really? Am I thinking about this correctly? Can I trust the claim? What does my life look like after? What's stopping me from saying yes? Why should I act right now? Do I like and trust who's speaking? Copy persuades when it answers the questions its goal needs, answers them truthfully, and the answers fit together. When one answer contradicts another, the reader feels that something is off and trusts everything else a little less.

The tools cover writing, reviewing and testing marketing copy, from ads and landing pages to emails, subject lines, social posts, headlines and scripts. plan_marketing_copy plans a piece around the questions its goal needs, and diagnose_marketing_copy reviews a draft against them. find_persuasion_techniques searches the catalog, and get_persuasion_technique returns one technique in full. check_headlines checks and compares headlines, hooks and subject lines, and check_marketing_claims checks claims and buttons. explain_why_not_converting works back from what a funnel shows to the likely cause. plan_ab_test sizes an A/B test, and read_ab_test_result reads its result.

Each technique comes with a link to its page, which shows the real examples behind it.
